items.name: Inaul
items.summary: Inaul is the handwoven cloth of the Maguindanaon; the word itself means "woven", and the cloth is mostly sold and worn as a malong. Its patterns are passed down in families, some are inspired by stories, objects or emotions, and some designs were once reserved for royal houses.
items.materials: Cotton (tanor), rayon and shiny katiyado thread; much of the silk thread is sourced from China
items.how_made: Women weave inaul on a hand loom (earlier weavers used backstrap looms); a length takes from 2 days to about 6 days for harder patterns. For the binaludan pattern the weaver dyes the threads, wraps them in banana leaves and dries them in the sun, a resist-dye method similar to ikat.
items.uses: Worn as the malong and also made into tubaw headcloths, shawls, headscarves, bags and gowns.

items.name: Malong a landap
items.summary: The malong a landap is the Maranao tube skirt made of broad plain-coloured panels joined by woven langkit bands. Handwoven landap are costly and worn at social functions, and their colours carry rank: yellow for sultans, red for warriors and green for imams.
items.materials: Silk or rayon, with cotton or rayon langkit bands
items.how_made: Separate panels are woven and joined into a tube by langkit strips, with 2 narrow tobrian strips running across and a single broader lakban down the middle. Langkit for the landap is woven on the backstrap loom, and in Tugaya the complex panels are made by needle-weaving.
items.uses: Worn by men and women as a skirt or wrap at weddings, feasts and other formal occasions.

items.name: Langkit
items.summary: Langkit are narrow, multicoloured woven strips that join and decorate the panels of a Maranao malong. A trained eye could once tell which part of the Lake Lanao region a person came from by the patterns of their malong and langkit.
items.how_made: The weaver chooses colours with the final pattern in mind, lays the threads on a warp board and moves them to a backstrap loom tied to a post, sitting on the floor and adjusting the tension with her back. Sequences are memorised without written manuals, and a seasoned weaver can finish a 1-metre langkit in a day.
items.uses: Sewn onto the malong a landap, and now also used on dresses, shirts, bookmarks, straps and table runners.

items.name: Yakan weaving
items.summary: Yakan tennun is the dense, brightly patterned woven cloth of the Yakan of Basilan, made in named categories such as the seputangan, sinaluan and bunga sama. The seputangan, worn by women at the waist or as a head cloth, is the most intricate design.
items.materials: Traditionally pineapple and abaca fibre coloured with plant dyes; chemical dyes are now common
items.how_made: Yakan weavers traditionally dyed plant fibres with extracts of leaves, roots and bark and wove them into geometric patterns, so that no two finished cloths are exactly alike. Chemical dyes and new products such as table runners and purses came with outside contact.
items.uses: Worn as head and waist cloths and as Yakan attire, notably in the Lami-Lamihan Festival parade.

items.name: Sama pandan mat
items.summary: Tepo are the pandan mats of the Sama of Tawi-Tawi, woven in stripes, multicoloured squares, checks and zigzags. Mats from Ungos Matata island in Tandubas are less pliable but more vivid in colour than the softer mats of Laminusa in Sulu.
items.how_made: Pandan leaves are harvested, dried, dyed and woven into designs. The craft is passed down among women, traditionally from mother to daughter.
items.uses: Used as sleeping and floor mats and often hung as wall decorations.

motifs.name: stripes, multicoloured squares, checks and zigzags

items.name: Maranao brass urn
items.summary: The gador is a lidded Maranao brass urn, cast in traditional forms and often made in pairs. Its silver-inlaid floral and geometric okir decoration is what sets Maranao brassware apart from that of the rest of island Southeast Asia.
items.materials: Brass or bronze, with silver inlay
items.how_made: Tugaya foundries cast gador by the lost-wax (cire perdue) method, then inlay silver-alloy patterns into the surface. The craft is concentrated in Tugaya's barangays of Lumbac, Bubong and Pandiaranao.
items.uses: Kept in Maranao homes, including the torogan, as containers for belongings, food and water.

motifs.name: okir
motifs.meaning: Maranao floral and geometric scroll designs, inlaid in silver

items.name: Maranao betel box
items.summary: The lotowan is a lidded brass box for betel nut and its ingredients, part of the Maranao betel (sireh) set. Museum pieces from Lanao del Sur are covered in silver-inlaid okir scrolls and flowers.
items.materials: Brass with silver inlay; some sets carry a beaded strap
items.how_made: The box is cast in brass and decorated by inlaying, stamping and incising silver designs. The silver-inlay technique is described as unique to Maranao brasswork.
items.uses: Holds betel nut and its ingredients as part of a betel (sireh) set.

motifs.meaning: geometric and floral designs drawn from Maranao woodcarving

items.name: Kulintang
items.summary: The kulintang is a row of 5 to 9 small knobbed gongs laid on a frame and played as the melody of an ensemble with larger hanging gongs and a drum. There is no fixed tuning, so every set has its own pitch, intervals and tone.
items.materials: Bronze traditionally, now mostly brass; wooden or bamboo frame
items.how_made: Each gong is cast by the lost-wax method in a mould of wax coated with powdered coal and mud, then tuned by ear by hammering the boss from inside or outside. The frame (antangan in Maguindanaon, langkonga in Maranao) can be carved with okir.
items.uses: Played at gatherings and festivals; traditionally a women's instrument, though men now play it too.

makers.name: Tugaya metalworkers
makers.note: Tugaya households make gongs, drums and other instruments.

items.name: Agung
items.summary: The agung is a pair of large, wide-rimmed hanging gongs that give the bass in a kulintang ensemble. It has a much deeper turned-in rim than the gandingan and usually weighs 13–16 pounds.
items.how_made: In Tugaya, agung are formed by hand, shaping and pounding flat metal sheets into solid gongs. The larger gong is the pangandungan (Maguindanaon) or p'nanggisa-an (Maranao), and the smaller, thicker one is the panentekan or p'malsan.
items.uses: Hung from a beam or stand and struck with padded mallets as the supporting bass of kulintang music.

makers.note: Hand-shape agong and gandingan from metal sheets.

items.name: Gandingan
items.summary: The gandingan is a set of four large, thin-rimmed hanging gongs that act as the second melody in the Maguindanaon kulintang ensemble. Played alone it imitates the tones of speech, so it is called the "talking gongs" and was used to send messages over distances.
items.materials: Bronze traditionally; now often steel or galvanised steel sheet
items.how_made: After World War II bronze became scarce, so many makers now cut the knob, body and rim from separate steel sheets, weld them and grind them smooth. Tugaya smiths also pound gandingan from flat metal sheets.
items.uses: Played standing with rubber-tipped mallets, in ensembles and in gandingan contests.

items.name: Kutiyapi
items.summary: The kutiyapi is a two-stringed, fretted boat lute about 4–6 feet long, carved from a single piece of soft wood. One string plays a constant drone while the other, an octave higher, carries the melody.
items.materials: Jackfruit or other soft wood; frets of hardened beeswax; rattan or plastic plectrum
items.how_made: The body is carved out of solid soft wood such as jackfruit and fitted with 9 frets of hardened beeswax.
items.uses: Played in dayunday song contests at weddings, Eid and other gatherings, and among the Maranao in courtship ensembles and to accompany epic chant.

items.name: Dabakan drum
items.summary: The dabakan is a single-headed goblet or hourglass drum, the only non-gong instrument of the Maguindanaon kulintang ensemble. Maranao makers carve the outside of the shell with okir.
items.materials: Coconut-trunk or jackfruit wood; goat, carabao, deer or lizard skin; rattan hoops
items.how_made: The shell is carved from coconut-trunk or jackfruit wood and hollowed out, and the skin is fastened with wire and two tight rattan hoops. Tugaya woodworkers also make the large dadabuan drum.
items.uses: Played with two thin rattan or bamboo sticks to keep the rhythm of kulintang music.

items.name: Okir woodcarving and inlaid chests
items.summary: Okir is the Maranao art of flowing plant-based scrolls, split into a curvilinear "male" style (okir-a-dato) and a geometric "female" style (okir-a-bai). In Tugaya it is carved into baul chests inlaid with polished shell and into drums, furniture and other woodwork.
items.how_made: Carvers cut okir designs into the wood, and every small piece of mother-of-pearl inlay is set by hand. Woodcarving and inlaid chests are made in Tugaya's barangays of Sugod-I, Ingud Poblacion, Dilimbayan and Tangcal.
items.uses: Baul chests store belongings and valuables; carved pieces decorate homes and are sold as heritage crafts.

makers.note: Master woodcarver whose Tugaya workshop makes baul with okir and tipay inlay; reported in 2024 that young people prefer other work.

makers.name: Alamin

makers.name: Ansary G. Bantayan

items.name: Torogan panolong
items.summary: Panolong are the large wing-like carved beam-ends that jut from the front of a torogan, the Maranao royal house. Modelled on the prows of Maranao boats, they make the house look like a royal vessel and are carved with the naga sea serpent and other okir.
items.how_made: Each panolong is carved with its own design, often an open-mouthed niyaga, with the sixth usually ending in a curling fern; torogan themselves are built without nails, using fitted joints and lashings.
items.uses: Mark the torogan of a datu as a symbol of rank and were meant to drive away evil spirits.

items.name: Sarimanok
items.summary: The sarimanok is the legendary bird of the Maranao, shown as a fowl with colourful wings and tail holding a fish in its beak or claws. It is the best-known symbol of Maranao art and stands for good fortune.
items.how_made: The head is profusely decorated with scroll, leaf and spiral motifs; because of Islamic beliefs against idolatry, living creatures in okir are deliberately stylised.
items.uses: Placed on top of poles with flags and standards during celebrations and on the umbrellas of sultans and dignitaries.

items.name: Kampilan
items.summary: The kampilan is a heritage long sword, 90–100 cm long, whose single-edged blade widens toward the tip. Its forked pommel is carved as a crocodile, sea serpent, hornbill or cockatoo.
items.how_made: The single-edged blade is laminated by pattern welding, and some blades have holes near the tip filled with brass.
items.uses: Survives as a heritage object and is central to the Maranao and Maguindanaon Sagayan war dance, which depicts a scene from the Darangen epic.

items.name: Kris sword
items.summary: The kalis is the Philippine kris: a double-edged sword, larger than the Javanese dagger, with a blade that is straight, wavy near the hilt or fully wavy. The kris appears on the flag of the Bangsamoro region as a symbol of Moro identity.
items.materials: Forged steel; hardwood pommel, sometimes with silver, brass or swasaa bands; rattan-bound hardwood scabbard
items.how_made: Traditional blades have deep waves forged to the centre line, while modern tourist pieces have shallow cut waves. In Tugaya, a 2007 report showed an older craftsman making blades in his workshop under his house.
items.uses: Kept as a heritage and ceremonial object and a symbol of Moro identity.

items.name: Sipil
items.summary: A brass box in five sections that keeps the apug, namat and maman of a betel chew clean. It carries the Maguindanaon custom of chewing betel nut.
items.uses: Holds what is needed for chewing betel nut.

items.name: Patakiya
items.summary: A brass vessel kept as a lemba, a piece for display, and set out at Maguindanaon celebrations, above all weddings.
items.uses: Displayed at weddings and other celebrations.

items.name: Dudan
items.summary: A vessel of galang, or brass, made for the custom of chewing and dipping tobacco.
items.uses: Used in chewing and dipping tobacco.

items.name: Langgaman
items.summary: A harvesting knife of steel and wood made to reach deep into thick rice stalks. Each harvest it is used for counts as a good one.
items.uses: Cutting rice at harvest.

items.name: Sayap and buyang
items.summary: The sayap is a wide-brimmed hat and the buyang a hand fan, both woven from palm leaves.
items.materials: Sayap: pandan, buri palm, coconut leaves, water hyacinth and other palms. Buyang: buri and anahaw palm.
items.uses: Everyday hat and fan.

items.name: Tudong
items.summary: A food cover woven from pandan dyed yellow, green, maroon and violet, stiffened underneath with coconut leaves and bamboo strips.
items.materials: Dyed pandan, coconut leaves and bamboo strips
items.uses: Keeps food warm and fresh at weddings, aqiqah, enthronements and other occasions.

items.name: Binangga
items.summary: A clay pot that held the water in Maguindanaon homes. The porous clay gave the water a taste of its own.
items.uses: Holding drinking water.

items.name: Sundang
items.summary: A Moro blade made straight (matidtu) or wavy (lanti), the waves likened to the flames of the naga, the mythical serpent. Maguindanaon warriors carried it.

images.author: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China
images.caption: Museum display of Moro swords: the labels identify the wavy-bladed and straight-bladed kris (kalis) as Maguindanao (Cotabato) and Maranao (Lanao del Sur) pieces. Museum of the Filipino People, Manila.

images.author: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China
images.caption: A Maranao kris with its wavy blade and ornate hilt, shown next to its sheath in the Bangsamoro gallery of the Museum of the Filipino People, Manila.

items.name: Binuwaya
items.summary: The blade of the highest-ranking Maguindanaon soldiers. Its three parts stand for three communities: Rajah Buayan in the blade, Datu Maguindanao in the middle and Sultan Kabuntalan in the handle.
items.uses: Now mostly carried in rituals, above all at weddings.

items.name: Babendil
items.summary: The timekeeper of the kulintang ensemble: a gong about a foot across, larger than the largest kulintang gong and near the size of the agong.
items.uses: Keeps time for the kulintang ensemble.

images.author: Philip Dominguez Mercurio (PhilipDM)
images.caption: A babendil, the small handheld gong that keeps time in the kulintang ensemble; this one is used by Maguindanaon master Danongan Kalanduyan to teach kulintang at San Francisco State.

images.author: Philip Dominguez Mercurio (PhilipDM)
images.caption: Another view of the babendil, the timekeeping gong of the kulintang ensemble, hung in its frame.

items.name: Obul-obul
items.summary: A Maguindanaon wedding decoration, hung with the pandala, sambulayang, bagiyuntay, pamanay and lansay, in many designs and bright colours.
items.uses: Decorates the wedding.

items.name: Gunong
items.summary: A Maranao dagger with a straight or curved blade, made for cutting and stabbing. Once a weapon, it is now kept as heritage.

images.author: Filhistorydotcom (filhistory.com)
images.caption: A gunong, the Moro dagger, at least 65 years old, with a laminated blade, a brass ferrule and guard, and a wooden sheath.

items.name: Igaan
items.summary: A Maranao bed: the frame carved with okir, the mattress, pillows and canopy trimmed with langkit.

items.name: Mamaan
items.summary: A brass betel-nut box decorated with okir, with a section each for the betel nut, the slaked lime and the betel leaf.
items.uses: Holds what is needed for chewing betel nut.

images.author: Hiart
images.caption: Maranao betel box of copper alloy with silver inlay, Mindanao, probably 20th century (Honolulu Museum of Art).

items.name: Mamandiyang
items.summary: A brightly coloured Maranao hanging in okir designs.
items.uses: Dresses Maranao homes, above all for weddings and sultanate enthronements.

items.name: Satora
items.summary: Maranao chess, played on a board of its own architectural layout. Sultans, datus and other respected people play it with family and friends, often in the torogan.
items.uses: A game for leisure.

items.name: Glat
items.summary: A cutting tool of everyday Maranao life, and a point of pride in its making.

items.name: Tanyak-tanyak
items.summary: The face painting of a Yakan wedding. White circles, dots, stars and other marks on the bride’s and groom’s faces and hands stand for heavenly witnesses to their vows.
items.materials: Borak sinah, a paste of rice flour and water
items.uses: Worn by the bride and groom at their wedding.

items.name: Yakan wedding dress
items.summary: At a Yakan wedding the couple dress in rich woven cloth and both wear tanyak-tanyak, a sign of love and harmony. The wedding is a community’s event as much as the couple’s.
items.uses: Worn by the bride and groom.

items.name: Yakan dress
items.local_name: pilis, kandit, sawwal; saputangan, badju lapih (Yakan)
items.summary: Men wear the pilis headdress, a red kandit cloth 10 to 15 metres long wound round the waist, and sawwal trousers finished with jambu tassels. Women wear the saputangan headscarf and the badju lapih, a blouse with close sleeves.

images.author: Valenzuela400
images.caption: A Yakan woman in traditional dress: a magenta badju blouse with rows of gold buttons, a striped woven wrap and belt, sawwal trousers and a woven head cloth; linked to master weaver Ambalang Ausalin of Lamitan, Basilan.

images.author: Valenzuela400
images.caption: Two Yakan women from a Basilan School of Living Tradition in green button-studded badju blouses, woven tennun wraps, striped trousers and head cloths.

motifs.name: jambu
motifs.meaning: the silk leg tassels of the sawwal, which stand for the horse and the place of horsemanship in Yakan life

items.name: Kulaing
items.summary: A jaw harp cut from a strip of bamboo about 2 centimetres wide.

items.name: Gabbang
items.summary: A xylophone of trapezoidal bamboo bars of different lengths set over a resonator, each bar carved to its own note and struck with mallets. It is played in Tawi-Tawi too, at dances, celebrations and gatherings.
items.uses: Accompanies songs and dances; children play it in the fields to scare off animals, birds and insects.

images.author: Icqgirl
images.caption: A gabbang, the bamboo xylophone of the Sulu archipelago, with its bamboo keys over a wooden box; owned by the University of the Philippines ensemble Kontra-Gapi.

images.author: Jfmrili
images.caption: A Tausug gabbang (bamboo xylophone) with its beater; property of UP Kontra-Gapi.

items.name: Suling
items.summary: A bamboo flute with carefully placed holes. Players learn both how to play it and what each melody means.

items.name: Barung
items.summary: The Yakan barung has a leaf-shaped blade carved with ukil near the edge and grip, a wooden pommel sheathed in silver, and a sheath set with old coins and tipay shell.
items.materials: Steel, wood, silver, coins and shell

items.name: Punyal
items.summary: A small kris for stabbing at close quarters, kept in a sheath and worn below the waist.

items.name: Bangka-bangka
items.summary: A boat-shaped container woven from pandan, for serving delicacies and fruit.
items.uses: Set out at weddings, at the completion of religious studies and on the Prophet’s birthday.

items.name: Dulang and latal
items.summary: A set of trays woven from nito vine for presenting delicacies and fruit, a sign of generosity and of Tawi-Tawi’s feasting tradition.

items.name: Habol tiyahian
items.summary: Cotton or silk cloth embroidered in bright DMC thread with ukkil or floral designs.
items.materials: Cotton or silk; DMC embroidery thread
items.uses: Worn by women at important events and festivals, with the batawi and sablay.

items.name: Kabkab
items.summary: A hand fan woven from pandan in intricate designs by the women of Sibutu.

items.name: Tutup
items.summary: A colourful food cover of pandan and bamboo strips in geometric patterns.
items.uses: Keeps dishes and delicacies fresh.

images.author: Valenzuela400
images.caption: A colourful woven tutup (food cover) labelled 'Tutup, Yakan SLT in Basilan'; this is a Yakan piece from Basilan, not Sama or Tausug from Tawi-Tawi.

images.author: Valenzuela400
images.caption: The same Yakan tutup (woven food cover) from Basilan, seen from above, with woven baskets beside it.

items.name: Kumpit
items.summary: A wooden boat that Tawi-Tawi’s islanders long relied on as their main way to travel, and a houseboat for the Sama-Badjao.

images.author: Patrick101456
images.caption: A lansa or kumpit, a large wooden Sama boat used to travel between the islands, moored on clear water.

items.name: Qur’an lihal
items.summary: A folding stand of carved mahogany that holds the Qur’an for reading and study. Tawi-Tawi is held to be where Islam first reached the archipelago.
items.uses: Holds the Qur’an for reading and study.

items.name: Sablay and sawwal
items.summary: Women’s dress: the long-sleeved sablay falls to the hips, its front covered by a simpay fastened with karusang pins, worn with patadjug or sawwal trousers and a kamban shawl or papanda scarf.

items.name: Sambra
items.summary: A short-sleeved blouse for every day, plainer than the batawi and sablay, in designs drawn from siyang batik.

items.name: Badju’ Sama
items.summary: Sama-Badjao dress in green and yellow, the colours of the Tawi-Tawi islands, and a sign of Sama-Badjao identity and pride.

festivals.name: Inaul Festival
festivals.note: Started in 2017 to promote inaul; features the Kapaginaul weaving competition, inaul gowns, a search for the oldest inaul and a trade expo. Reporting found covers 2017–2019.

festivals.name: Lami-Lamihan Festival
festivals.note: Opens on June 26 at the Datu Kalun Shrine; a celebration of Yakan culture with a parade in hand-woven Yakan attire. 2025 was its 42nd year.

festivals.name: Shariff Kabunsuan Festival
festivals.note: Mid-December; highlight is the Guinakit fluvial parade on December 19 along the Rio Grande de Mindanao, with ornately adorned boats once used by royal families.

festivals.name: Langkit Festival
festivals.note: Week-long city charter celebration named after the langkit, with barangay booths, kulintang playing and a langkit competition.

festivals.name: Okir Art Exhibit
festivals.note: BARMM trade ministry exhibit of Maranao baul, tapestries, paintings and okir jewellery; held in April 2024.

festivals.name: National Arts and Crafts Fair
festivals.note: National crafts fair where a pandan mat weaver from Mapun, Tawi-Tawi, wove at her booth in 2025.

notes: Dropped: ornament/jewellery group (no source on Maranao or Maguindanaon gold, beadwork or headdresses could be read; only an LLM-generated page and slide decks turned up). Malong a andon dropped (only a passing mention in Wikipedia). Teduray and Iranun weaving (no readable source; a Commons caption names an Iranun Weaving Center in Sultan Kudarat but was not used as a fact source). Yakan music (Uwang Ahadas, GAMABA 2000, Lamitan: gabbang, kwintangan) left out because no free image of Yakan instruments was found. Kubing jaw harp and pira (Yakan sword) left out as too thinly sourced. Barong sword and Tausug pis syabit excluded as Sulu crafts; Darhata Sawabi (Parang, Sulu) excluded. Kalilang festival dropped (no source found). Rasid Laidon, named in a search snippet as a Tugaya brass caster and 1990 awardee, is not in the NCCA GAMABA list on Wikipedia and was not used. Blocked or not read: NCCA (403), PNA article URLs (404), PCIJ needed an expired-certificate bypass; Inquirer, MindaNews and PIA skipped per instructions, so the Inquirer price for Yakan cloth (P400 a metre) was not used. The inaul price (PTV, February 2018) is the only price stated by a news source; Inaul Festival coverage stops at 2019, so its current schedule after the 2022 split of Maguindanao is unconfirmed. Province is a single slug: inaul is woven in both Maguindanao provinces (Buluan and Datu Piang in del Sur; Sultan Kudarat and Sultan Mastura in del Norte). Towns are left empty where no source says where an item is made. Colours are judgement from photos. Image urls: Commons no longer serves 1600px thumbnails (a 1600px request returns HTTP 400); the API returns its 1920px bucket on thumb.wikimedia.org, or the original file when it is narrower than that, and width/height match the url given.
